newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil re-election bill faces 2nd lower house vote.
newsitem.headline: Brazil re-election bill faces 2nd lower house vote.

text.p: A constitutional amendment allowing Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to run for re-election next year will be put to a second vote in the Chamber of Deputies on Tuesday, a congressional official said.

The government is confident of a bigger margin of victory than in a first lower house vote in January when 336 deputies voted in favor of the re-election bill, an aide to the government's chief whip Dep. Benito Gama said.
As a constitutional amendment the legislation requires two three-fifths majorities, each equivalent to 308 votes, before advancing to the Senate.
In January, the government struggled to overcome opposition to the timing of the re-election bill within allied parties and only managed to hold a vote on the amendment at a third attempt.

Since then, inter-party tensions have subsided following the elections of the new presidents of Congress' two houses and no significant opposition is expected before Tuesday's scheduled vote, Gama's aide said.
Should re-election be approved, government-allied parties in Congress will spend much of the remainder of the week negotiating who gets to run which committees.
The top jobs in Congress' committees are renewed every two years and are usually hogged by the two biggest parties, the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party and the Liberal Front Party.

This year, however, Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party appears to have won itself a better share of the panel posts after it threatened to ally itself with another party and become top dog in Congress.

While party leaders haggle, a special committee mulling a bill regulating the opening of Brazil's petroleum monopoly were due to vote on the legislation on Tuesday, although that session may be delayed because of the scheduled re-election vote.
The week in Brasilia is also likely to be dominated by an ongoing inquiry by a Senate committee into an alleged, multi-million-dollar fraud involving state and municipal debt.
Last week, the Central Bank closed more than a dozen financial institutions accused of buying underpriced bonds and selling them on in successive operations for quick profit.
The issuers of the bonds are also under investigation for allegedly underpricing their debt and using the funds for purposes other than their stated purpose of meeting court settlements.
